reviews.title: Chapter 1 textbook review

questions.label: Q1, Q2, Q4, Q14–16 on printed pp. 30–31

guides: Q1 · Decomposers
Decomposers obtain organic carbon and chemical energy from existing organic matter. They do not become autotrophs merely because they recycle nutrients.
Q2 · Vent producers
Chemosynthetic producers use energy released by chemical reactions to build organic matter from inorganic carbon. Their energy source differs from the light used by photosynthetic producers.
Q4 · Transfer assumption
Ten percent is a simplifying assumption, not a fixed law. Actual transfer varies with what is eaten, assimilation, respiration, the organisms and the measurement boundary.
Q14 · Caterpillar budget
Of 200 J ingested, 100 J leaves in feces and 67 J is used in respiration. The 33 J retained as growth is 16.5% of 200 J; 83.5%, approximately 85%, is not retained as new biomass.
Q15 · Inverted biomass
A small standing stock of phytoplankton can reproduce and be consumed rapidly. A biomass snapshot is not a measurement of energy transferred per unit time.
Q16 · Pyramid of numbers
Many grass plants can support fewer herbivores; one large tree can support many insects. Counting organisms ignores their individual sizes.

reviews.title: Chapter 2 textbook review

questions.label: Q2, Q5, Q8, Q11, Q12 and Q17 on printed p. 64

guides: Q2 and Q5 · Water

Polarity supports interactions with ions and other polar molecules. Hydrogen bonding supports cohesion and contributes to water's temperature-buffering properties. The open structure of ice makes it less dense than liquid water; water is not literally a solvent for every substance.
Q8 · Nutrient enrichment

Added phosphorus can stimulate growth when it is limiting. More organic matter can support more microbial respiration during decomposition, reducing dissolved oxygen. Light, mixing and other conditions also matter.
Q11 · Nitrogen transformations

Plants commonly take up ammonium and nitrate. Fixation introduces biologically available nitrogen; nitrification converts ammonium through nitrite to nitrate. Denitrification returns nitrogen to gaseous forms. Assimilation is incorporation into organic molecules.
Q12 · Acid deposition
Sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides can form acids through atmospheric reactions. Sulfur and nitrogen cycles are involved; sources, transport and ecosystem buffering affect the resulting harm.
Q17 · Nitrogen diagram

Include atmospheric nitrogen, fixation, ammonium, nitrification, nitrate, assimilation, organic nitrogen, decomposition and denitrification. Label the arrows as processes rather than treating all pathways as the same step.

reviews.title: Unit A — Textbook Unit 1 review

questions.label: Q1, Q3, Q9, Q21 and Q30 on printed pp. 68–70

guides: Q1 and Q3 · Energy sources

A terrestrial pathway usually begins with light captured by producers. A vent pathway may begin with chemical energy used by chemosynthetic producers. Both involve transfers through organisms and dissipation as heat.
Q9 · Beetle budget

The beetle retains 17% of 750 J as growth: 0.17 × 750 = 127.5 J. Under the question's simplified boundary, that growth is the energy potentially available in its biomass to the next level; ingestion is not guaranteed.
Q21 · Two transfers

Using the stipulated 10% assumption, plant to caterpillar transfers 250 J and caterpillar to meat transfers 25 J. This calculation follows the source's assumed feeding chain and is not a measured universal efficiency.
Q30 · Matter and energy

Atoms are rearranged and transferred among reservoirs; energy is transferred and transformed, with increasing dispersal as heat. Energy is conserved, but usable energy does not cycle through the ecosystem in the same way as matter.
